desc:
A country has n cities numbered 0 to n - 1. Each entry roads[i] = [a, b, toll] is a two-way road between cities a and b with the given toll. In addition, every city v charges an entry fee fees[v] to every traveller who is in it, including the city you start in and the city you end in. If a route visits a city twice, the fee is paid twice.

Return the smallest total cost (all tolls plus all city fees along the route) of travelling from src to dst, or -1 if there is no route. If src == dst the cost is just fees[src].

n = 4, src = 0, dst = 3, fees = [1, 10, 2, 1]
roads = [[0,1,1], [1,3,1], [0,2,3], [2,3,3]]
via city 1: 1 + 1 + 10 + 1 + 1 = 14
via city 2: 1 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 10
-> 10
hints: The cost lives on cities as well as on roads. Think about which of the two is easier to turn into the other.
Charge each city's fee when you enter it: moving along a road to city v costs toll + fees[v]. The start city's fee is paid up front.
Now every step has a positive cost, so run ordinary Dijkstra from src with initial distance fees[src] and edge weight toll + fees[v].
editorial: Node weights can be folded into edge weights. Every route enters each city after the first through exactly one road, so assign the fee of the destination city to that road: the weight of travelling u -> v becomes toll + fees[v], and the fee of the start city is added once as the initial distance. The total of such weights along a route equals tolls plus fees of every visited city.

All new weights are at least 1 (tolls are positive), so Dijkstra applies directly. Because the fee is paid for every visit, a route that revisits a city is never better, which is consistent with a shortest path being simple.
Remember to make the roads two-way, to initialise dist[src] = fees[src] (not 0), and to treat -1 for an unreachable destination. Time O((V + E) log E).
